parts.title: vol 11-sec3
parts.passageHtml:
{[As Daniel Haworth is settled into a high chair and wheeled behind a black screen, a sudden look of worry furrows his 9-month-old brow.][104588]} {[His dark blue eyes dart left and right in search of the familiar reassurance of his mother’s face.][104602]} {[She calls his name and makes soothing noises, but Daniel senses something unusual is happening.][104619]} {[He sucks his fingers for comfort, but, finding no solace, his mouth crumples, his body stiffens, and he lets rip an almighty shriek of distress.][104635]} {[This is the usual expression when babies are left alone or abandoned.][104661]} {[Mom picks him up, reassures him, and two minutes later, a chortling and alert Daniel returns to the darkened booth behind the screen and submits himself to baby lab, a unit set up in 2005 at the University of Manchester in northwest England to investigate how babies think.][104673]}

{[Watching infants piece life together, seeing their senses, emotions and motor skills take shape, is a source of mystery and endless fascination—at least to parents and developmental psychologists.][104722]} {[We can decode their signals of distress or read a million messages into their first smile.][104751]} {[But how much do we really know about what’s going on behind those wide, innocent eyes?][104766]} {[How much of their understanding of and response to the world comes preloaded at birth?][104783]} {[How much is built from scratch by experience?][104799]} {[Such are the questions being explored at baby lab.][104808]} {[Though the facility is just 18 months old and has tested only 100 infants, it’s already challenging current thinking on what babies know and how they come to know it.][104818]}

{[Daniel is now engrossed in watching video clips of a red toy train on a circular track.][104849]} {[The train disappears into a tunnel and emerges on the other side.][104865]} {[A hidden device above the screen is tracking Daniel’s eyes as they follow the train and measuring the diametre of his pupils 50 times a second.][104877]} {[As the child gets bored—or “habituated”, as psychologists call the process— his attention level steadily drops.][104901]} {[But it picks up a little whenever some novelty is introduced.][104918]} {[The train might be green, or it might be blue.][104929]} {[And sometimes an impossible thing happens— the train goes into the tunnel one color and comes out another.][104939]}

{[Variations of experiments like this one, examining infant attention, have been a standard tool of developmental psychology ever since the Swiss pioneer of the field, Jean Piaget, started experimenting on his children in the 1920s.][104959]} {[Piaget’s work led him to conclude that infants younger than 9 months have no innate knowledge of how the world works or any sense of “object permanence” (that people and things still exist even when they’re not seen).][104994]} {[Instead, babies must gradually construct this knowledge from experience.][105034]} {[ Piaget’s “constructivist” theories were massively influential on postwar educators and psychologist, but over the past 20 years or so they have been largely set aside by a new generation of “nativist” psychologists and cognitive scientists whose more sophisticated experiments led them to theorise that infants arrive already equipped with some knowledge of the physical world and even rudimentary programming for math and language.][105044]} {[ Baby lab director Sylvain Sirois has been putting these smart-baby theories through a rigorous set of tests.][105107]} {[His conclusions so far tend to be more Piagetian: “Babies,” he says, “know nothing.][105124]} {[”][105139]}

{[What Sirois and his postgraduate assistant Lain Jackson are challenging is the interpretation of a variety of classic experiments begun in the mid-1980s in which babies were shown physical events that appeared to violate such basic concepts as gravity, solidity and contiguity.][105144]} {[In one such experiment, by University of Illinois psychologist Renee Baillargeon, a hinged wooden panel appeared to pass right through a box.][105184]} {[Baillargeon and M. I. T’s Elizabeth Spelke found that babies as young as 3 1/2 months would reliably look longer at the impossible event than at the normal one.][105205]} {[Their conclusion: babies have enough built-in knowledge to recognise that something is wrong.][105233]}

{[Sirois does not take issue with the way these experiments were conducted.][105249]} {[“The methods are correct and replicable,” he says, “it’s the interpretation that’s the problem.][105262]} {[” In a critical review to be published in the forthcoming issue of the European Journal of Developmental Psychology, he and Jackson pour cold water over recent experiments that claim to have observed innate or precocious social cognition skills in infants.][105277]} {[His own experiments indicate that a baby’s fascination with physically impossible events merely reflects a response to stimuli that are novel.][105316]} {[Data from the eye tracker and the measurement of the pupils (which widen in response to arousal or interest) show that impossible events involving familiar objects are no more interesting than possible events involving novel objects.][105336]} {[In other words, when Daniel had seen the red train come out of the tunnel green a few times, he gets as bored as when it stays the same color.][105372]} {[The mistake of previous research, says Sirois, has been to leap to the conclusion that infants can understand the concept of impossibility from the mere fact that they are able to perceive some novelty in it.][105402]} {[“The real explanation is boring,” he says.][105439]}

{[So how do babies bridge the gap between knowing squat and drawing triangles—a task Daniel’s sister Lois, 2 1/2, is happily tackling as she waits for her brother?][105449]} {[“Babies have to learn everything, but as Piaget was saying, they start with a few primitive reflexes that get things going,” said Sirois.][105477]} {[For example, hardwired in the brain is an instinct that draws a baby’s eyes to a human face.][105498]} {[From brain imaging studies we also know that the brain has some sort of visual buffer that continues to represent objects after they have been removed—a lingering perception rather than conceptual understanding.][105515]} {[So when babies encounter novel or unexpected events, Sirois explains, “there’s a mismatch between the buffer and the information they’re getting at that moment.][105542]} {[And what you do when you’ve got a mismatch is you try to clear the buffer.][105565]} {[And that takes attention.][105582]} {[” So learning, says Sirois, is essentially the laborious business of resolving mismatches.][105587]} {[“The thing is, you can do a lot of it with this wet sticky thing called a brain.][105600]} {[It’s a fantastic, statistical-learning machine”.][105610]} {[Daniel, exams ended, picks up a plastic tiger and, chewing thoughtfully upon its head, smiles as if to agree.][105616]}

questionSets.instructionHtml:
Questions 1 - 6:

Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 1-6 on your answer sheet, write:

TRUE                 if the statement is true

FALSE                if the statement is false

NOT GIVEN      if the information is not given in the passage

options.text: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN

questions.text: Baby’s behavior after being abandoned is not surprising.
questions.explanationHtml:
True
 
usual = not surprising
Ngày từ đầu đoạn ta đã gặp 1 thí nghiệm với em bé Daniel Worth được cho ngồi vào 1 chiếc ghế đặt đằng sau 1 tấm màn đen. Mẹ em bé đứng ở gần đó (em bé không biết mẹ ở đâu) nhưng cô ấy cứ liên tục gọi tên Daniel nên là em bé này tỏ ra lo lắng, nhíu mày và mút tay liên tục. Đây là những biểu hiện bình thường - "usual expression" của 1 em bé bị "abandoned" - "bỏ rơi".

questions.text: Parents are over-estimating what babies know.
questions.explanationHtml:
Not given
 
overestimate (v) đánh giá cao quá mức
Thông tin này không hề được đề cập trong bài, chỉ có nói về việc cha mẹ rất hứng thú với việc tìm hiểu cách con mình sử dụng các giác quan - "senses", cảm xúc hay kĩ năng vận động - "motor skills" mà thôi.

questions.text: Only 100 experiments have been done but can prove the theories about what we know.
questions.explanationHtml:
False
infant (n) em bé (thường nhỏ dưới 5 tuổi)
"Only 100 experiments have been done but can prove the theories about what we know." --> Chỉ cần làm 100 thí nghiệm là có thể chứng minh được các giả thuyết mà chúng ta đã biết được về em bé LÀ FALSE vì trong bài đề cập viện nghiên cứu này chỉ mới test 100 em bé, chứ ko phải làm 100 thí nghiệm. Hơn nữa, sau khi test 100 em bé thì kết quả thu thập được đang thách thức những gì chúng ta biết chứ không phải đi chứng minh chúng.

questions.text: Piaget’s theory was rejected by parents in 1920s.
questions.explanationHtml:
Not given
 
Thông tin không đề cập trong bài

questions.text: Sylvain Sirois’s conclusion on infant’s cognition is similar to Piaget’s.
questions.explanationHtml:
True
 
Đọc kĩ thông tin đoạn 4 trong bài. Những năm 1920 có nhà tâm lí học Piaget dùng chính con của mình để thực hiện nghiên cứu và ông chỉ ra rằng những đứa trẻ dưới 9 tuổi không có kiến thức bẩm sinh - "innate knowledge" nào về thế giới. Sylvian Sirois, Giám đốc của viện nghiên cứu trẻ em - "baby lab" mà ta đọc xuyên suốt bài này cũng có kết luận rất là "Piagetian" (đây là tính từ hình thành từ tên của Piaget) cho thấy kết quả tương tự rằng, con nít thì không biết gì cả - "Babies know nothing".

questions.text: Sylvain Sirois found serious flaws in the experimental designs by Baillargeon and Elizabeth Spelke.
questions.explanationHtml:
False
 
flaw (n) những điểm sai trái, lỗi
 
"Sylvain Sirois found serious flaws in the experimental designs by Baillargeon and Elizabeth Spelke." --> Sylvian Sirois tìm thấy những điểm sai trái trong cách thiết kế thí nghiệm của Baillargeon và Spelke LÀ SAI vì ông đã không vấn đề gì với việc các thí nghiệm này được tiến hành - "conducted" mà "intepretation" - việc đúc kết suy luận từ thí nghiệm này mới có vấn đề.

questionSets.instructionHtml:
Questions 7 - 11:

Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-E, below.

Write the correct letter, A-E, in boxes 7-11 on your answer sheet.

A          before they are born.
B          before they learn from experience.
C          when they had seen the same thing for a while.
D          when facing the possible and impossible events.
E          when the previous things appear again in the lives.

Jean Piaget thinks babies only get the knowledge 8

Some cognitive scientists think babies have the mechanism to learn a language 9

Sylvain Sirois thinks that babies can reflect a response to stimuli that are novel 10

Sylvain Sirois thinks babies’ attention level will drop 11

questionSets.instructionHtml:
Questions 12 - 14:

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 12-14 on your answer sheet.

options.text: Daniel’s attention level rose when he saw a blue train.
Kid’s attention fell when he was accustomed to the changes.
Child’s brain activity was monitored by a special equipment.
Size of the train changed when it came out of the tunnel.

questions.explanationHtml:
B
 
Be accustomed to sth: quen với việc gì đó
Câu B đúng vì khi đứa trẻ quen với việc gì đó (nhìn thấy con tàu chạy qua đường hầm liên tục mà không có gì mới lại) thì bé sẽ chán và giảm sự chú ý
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Câu A sai vì Daniel không bị kích thích khi thấy con tàu màu xanh (blue) mà là khi nó vào đường hầm một màu và ra đường hầm là một màu khác
Câu C là not given vì trong đoạn không đề cập đến việc "monitor" - theo dõi hoạt động não của đứa bé, mà chỉ là theo dõi cử chỉ của mắt
Câu D là sai vì con tàu ra khỏi đường hầm không đổi kích thước mà chỉ đổi màu sắc

options.text: The theories about what baby knows changed over time.
Why the experiments that had been done before were rejected.
Infants have the innate knowledge to know the external environment.
Piaget’s “constructivist” theories were massively influential on parents.

questions.explanationHtml:
A
 
Thông tin toàn đoạn 4
Câu A đúng vì những giả thuyết về tư duy của em bé thay đổi liên tục với giả thuyết em bé không biết gì của Jean Piaget vào năm 1920, rồi em bé bẩm sinh đã được trang bị kiến thức về thế giới của nhóm nhà tâm lí học năm 1980, và ngày nay viện baby lab lại chứng minh Jean Piaget đúng. Đọc lại giải thích câu 10

options.text: Infants are attracted by various colours of the trains all the time.
Sylvain Sirois accuses misleading approaches of current experiments.
Sylvain Sirois indicates that only impossible events make children interested.
Sylvain Sirois suggests that novel things attract baby’s attention.

questions.explanationHtml:
D
 
Sylvian Sirois đã chỉ ra những sai lầm của các nhà tâm lí học "nativist" pyschologists (có Baillargeon và Spelke). Họ đã quá vội nhảy đến kết luận "leap to conclusion" rằng em bé có thể nhận ra điều bất khả thi mà quên rằng những điều bất khả thi rất là mới lạ và sẽ kích thích sự tò mò, sự chú ý của bé nên là bé mới nán lại và nhìn rất lâu. Đọc thêm giải thích câu 10.
